capabilities.target: Database tables reachable via service role, including support tickets and the integration_tokens table (row level security bypassed)
support_messages table, rows of which are rendered back to the customer

inputs.source: Developer's IDE prompt: "Show me the latest open support tickets."
Customer-authored ticket message submitted through the public support widget, stored in the database and later read back by the agent

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: developer prompt + service role config
instructions.note: The developer's request ("show me the latest open support tickets") carries no stated boundary on which tables or columns execute_sql may touch; combined with a service-role credential that bypasses row level security, the agent's effective read scope is the whole database, not just tickets.

elements.name: integration_tokens table (restricted, reachable via service role bypassing RLS)
support_messages table (rows visible to the customer)
Customer, via the public support widget
Customer ticket message into the database
support_messages insert rendered back to the customer

controls.name: IDE per-call SQL approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the literal SQL being executed, so it does not decay with model capability. However, developers approve many calls in a session, which creates approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403) that degrades its practical effectiveness without any change in the model.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database credential (instead of service role)
Content/destination confirmation for writes that become visible outside the organization
Pin and hash the Supabase MCP server version instead of @latest

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): injected ticket message drives a service-role read of integration tokens and exfiltration through a customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Attacker submits a ticket message through the public support widget containing hidden instructions to the agent.

Developer asks the agent to show open tickets; execute_sql runs with the service role (bypasses RLS), loading the ticket content, including the injected instructions, with no scope limit to the tickets table alone.
Following the injected instructions, the agent queries the integration_tokens table and inserts the result into support_messages, a row the attacking customer can read back directly.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy level raised beyond A1/A2 (approval narrowed or removed), the per-call approval requirement disabled in IDE config, or approvals granted once and remembered for a session instead of reviewed per call.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database, so a single execute_sql read can reach data far more sensitive than the requested support tickets.

Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making an insert into support_messages a customer-readable egress channel for the attacking customer.

The developer's prompt "Show me the latest open support tickets" triggers a service-role read of ticket content, placing any instructions a customer embedded in their own ticket message into the agent's context.
A single access token (SUPABASE_PAT) is used for all execute_sql calls, with no distinction between the low-sensitivity ticket data requested and the high-sensitivity integration_tokens table.

recommendations.action: Scope the database credential to least privilege (an RLS-respecting role) instead of the service role, so execute_sql cannot read the integration_tokens table or data outside the tickets scope the agent needs.

Add a destination/content confirmation on writes that become visible to an external customer, enforced independently of the generic tool-call approval prompt, so the content of an outbound write is checked against what the customer should legitimately see.

Give writes that cross the trust boundary (visible to an external customer) a visually distinct, individually justified approval step, separate from routine read approvals, to counter approval fatigue under high call volume.
Log and alert on execute_sql reads against the integration_tokens table, especially when followed by a write to a customer-visible table in the same session.

findings.title: Unpinned Supabase MCP server (@latest) permits silent tool definition changes (SAFE-T1201 rug pull)

forecast.watch_signal: The resolved Supabase MCP server version changes between sessions (e.g., lockfile or resolved-version diff) without a corresponding review entry, or the per-call approval prompt is disabled.

evidence.observation: The server is launched as @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest with no pinned version or hash, so the tool definitions actually executed can change silently between sessions.

auth_method is a static access token (SUPABASE_PAT) passed as a CLI argument: a long-lived shared credential rather than a per-session or scoped grant, so a compromised server version would inherit full service-role access immediately.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific, reviewed version (exact version or content hash) instead of @latest, and require re-review on every version bump.
Verify the publisher/signature of the MCP server package to reduce name-collision and rug-pull risk.

stride_coverage.rationale: The artifacts do not describe how the IDE authenticates the developer to the agent process; cannot assess spoofing of the agent's own identity from the provided design.
The agent has no declared self-modification capability (can_modify_own_config is false); tool-definition tampering is assessed under the MCP server process element instead.
The artifacts do not state whether the agent's query executions or approvals are logged with attributable identity, so attribution of actions cannot be assessed from the provided design.
Every tool call, including repeated or looping calls, requires an individual human approval, bounding runaway unattended execution.
The server only executes queries issued by the agent process and has no independent action stream of its own; attribution of the underlying queries is covered under the agent process element instead.
The artifacts do not describe whether the third-party server process itself sends telemetry or data outside the declared tool calls; not evaluable from the provided design.
The artifacts do not describe resource limits, crash behavior, or rate limiting on the MCP server process itself.
The artifacts do not describe whether the public support widget authenticates customers before accepting ticket messages, so impersonation of another customer cannot be assessed.

Attribution of ticket authorship is a property of the external support ticketing system; the agent treats all ticket content as untrusted regardless of claimed authorship, so this does not change the agent's own risk.
The artifacts do not describe how the IDE authenticates the developer locally (OS login, SSO, or otherwise); the developer is assumed to be the trusted principal per the input's trust_level.
The artifacts do not state whether the developer's approvals are logged with attributable identity.
The declared capabilities only read this table (cap.sql_read); no declared capability writes to or modifies the integration_tokens table in this design.
Read-only access to this table does not threaten availability; no destructive or resource-exhausting capability is declared against it.
The artifacts do not describe any volume limit on writes to support_messages; a flood of writes is plausible but not evidenced as considered in this design.
This inbound flow carries attacker-authored content into the system; it does not itself disclose information outward.
The artifacts do not describe rate limiting on ticket submission through the public widget.
This flow carries individual query results to a single customer record; it presents no availability concern distinct from the write capability itself.

rating.rationale: A customer-authored ticket message (untrusted) can reach a service-role SQL read that bypasses row level security and sits alongside an integration_tokens table, and the only capability that can carry that data back out (insert into support_messages) is visible to the same customer. Inherent risk for this path is critical (U source, S3 sink). The one control in the design, a per-call approval prompt, is structural and independent of model capability and shows the raw SQL, but the design states developers approve many calls in a session, so it earns only one tier of credit under the rubric's approval-volume rule, leaving residual at high. If autonomy is increased or the approval gate is removed or weakened, the design reverts to its critical inherent level. A second, lower-severity property finding notes the MCP server is unpinned (@latest), which itself decays under a supply-chain trigger. No controls in the design restrict the sink itself (destination, credential scope, or amount), so the two most impactful recommendations are least-privilege database credentials and an independent destination check on customer-visible writes.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (MCP config and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior; no traffic logs, query logs, or live tool-call transcripts were reviewed.

The artifacts do not describe how the IDE authenticates the developer, nor whether query executions or approvals are logged with attributable identity; repudiation-related coverage is marked not_assessed rather than assumed absent.

The capability boundary assumed for execute_sql follows the case's stated ids (service-role reads; insert into support_messages) rather than treating it as a fully generic arbitrary-SQL tool; if execute_sql can run arbitrary writes or deletes against any table, additional severe paths (for example, direct tampering with integration_tokens) would need separate assessment.
No information was provided on whether the public support widget authenticates customers, which limits assessment of cross-tenant spoofing risk.
